title: Amazing Game!! London System Analysis | Jobava London | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We have the Black pieces against a good player. As promised, I'm going into my main repertoire. d4, the knight to f6.
The knight to c3 — we might be facing a Jobava London here.
The knight to c3 is the introductory move; I'll oblige with d5, and this is going to be a very interesting twist.

Of course the bishop to f4 isn't the only move, and we are indeed facing the Jobava London — I'm now Black against my own opening, but I won't hold back, I'll give my honest recommendations. What you should understand about the Black side of the Jobava is that there are seven or eight equalising lines — it's impossible to say that e6 is worse than the bishop to f5, or a6 worse than e6; all the typical moves here, other than the knight to c6, which blunders the knight to b5, are approximately equivalent in objective strength. 'Best' is relative — each line leads to a different type of position, and whichever you play, you have to know it well, because almost every move is good. Even the relatively rare c6 is quite decent. The move that's probably easiest for most people to understand, because it's also the most forcing —
and you could call it the most principled — is the direct central strike, c5. You're basically trying to punish White directly for bringing the knight out to c3.
In the traditional London, how is c5 often met? With the move c3, to reinforce the d4-pawn. So you're trying to highlight
the fact that White has brought the knight out to c3, and the d4-pawn has now become a serious target, which we are

directly assaulting with the move c5. e4 is of course the move in the Jobava London course, so we follow one of its main lines. There are three main moves here, all analysed very deeply: c-takes-d4, d-takes-c4, and the one I'll play in this game,

the most forcing line, and currently considered the most reputable within c5 — take on e4 with the knight, to force the knights off the board before White plays d-takes-c5. So the knight takes e4; White of course
will recapture on e4, the only feasible move. Take note that the knight to b5 is not dangerous as long
as the knight remains on b8 — this is an important point, because it can always

be met with the defensive knight to a6. Now we trade on e4; White will re-establish material equality with d-takes-c5. In the old days, when the Jobava was first appearing and this e4 move came to the fore, people
actually played this gambit-style, by advancing the pawn to d5, kind of like a Falkbeer Counter-Gambit, as I'll show after the game,
but it was quickly determined, with the aid of computers, that d5 is unsound — White has woefully insufficient compensation for the pawn — so people switched to

d-takes-c5. There's a fork in the road: there's the queen takes d1 with check, which leads to a fascinating endgame, an equal one but very difficult for Black to play practically; and the second move,
which we're going to play — the queen to a5 with check, forking the king and the c5-pawn, going down one of the most topical lines of the course and of the Jobava in general.

We didn't invent this line — it's in everybody's course, because e4 is the standard recommendation these days by most Jobava London authors. Of course there's also the old-school move e3, which I'll talk about after the game and explain why I don't really recommend it for Jobava aficionados. So the queen takes c5, and of course we're expecting the queen to a4 with check — that's precisely why White blocks the check with the pawn, so that the diagonal is open for the queen and White is able to win back the e4-pawn. It's interesting that our opponent is taking sizable chunks of time on every move — it tells me they may not be totally familiar with the theory, or are just trying to remember it. The queen to a4 with check — how do we block this check? Do we play the bishop to d7, or the knight to c6? Newer players might look at one of these.
